title: Death is Not A Great Consumer Experience
subtitle: Approaching the inevitable with an eye towards satisfaction.
body_html:
The net promoter score is commonly used across industries to measure customer satisfaction. You ask your customers to rate their experience with your product on a scale:

  1. How likely are you to recommend our product/service to a friend or colleague?”
    They answer on a scale from 0 to 10.

  2. Categorize responses:

    • Promoters (9–10): Loyal enthusiasts.

    • Passives (7–8): Satisfied but unenthusiastic.

    • Detractors (0–6): Unhappy customers.

  3. Calculate percentages:

    • % of respondents who are Promoters

    • % who are Detractors

  4. Then you'll apply this formula

NPS = % Promoters – % Detractors

For some reason, I haven't seen the NPS for death.

Part of that may be that 100% of potential promoters and 100% of potential detractors have all passed into the great beyond.

My dear friend . She is sitting at the bedside of her mom, only a very short period after her father died. Her mother is not going to make it. Over a long enough time scale, none of us make it. This is a cold and lonely experience, only made worse because none of us can meaningfully prepare for an event so inevitable, yet so awful.

Death is a constant of the human experience. Unfortunately, given the sharp precipice between being and not being that all of us fall off, it's tough to get empirical data about how satisfying the experience of death is for customers, which is all of us, of the experience of life inevitably ending. We are left with the less satisfying data of death observers, a hypothesis about what the death experience may or may not be like.

Not satisfied with just trying to write this column from my own brain, I decided to call my friend Lila, who's coping with death right now, to ask her what she thought about death from a customer experience standpoint:

Owen

You inspired me to try to create something mild to moderately amusing about that poor customer experience, which is death.

Lila Donnolo

Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha yes please

Owen

OK, so I intend that since—wait, do you know the net promoter score?

Lila Donnolo

No

Owen

In business, broadly, we have this concept of a net promoter score. We ask people if they can rate the customer experience between one and 10, and then we take people who rate it as a nine or 10. They're promoters, and then you subtract people who rate it any lower than 6, so you have a percentage of promoters versus detractors, and the people in the middle don't count really. So it's like then it's so like, for example, United Healthcare is -12, on a scale of 1 to 100.

Lila Donnolo

Of course

Owen

And in my clinic, it’s like in the 90s, like Apple is the gold standard at 72, but we don't have a net promoter…

Lila Donnolo

OK, OK

Owen

…score for death, and so we were left to talk to basically, cause we all know when we're dead, we can't report back whether it was good or bad as a

Lila Donnolo

Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha

Owen

customer and so we don't know…

Lila Donnolo

What products or services are we using?

Owen

Death is a product and a service, but we have to ask people who observe the customer experience. You're one of those people, so I'm going to ask you about the “death customer experience.”

Lila Donnolo

Yes, zero out of 10 would recommend Awful. It's hard, it's awful,

Owen

So you're a detractor.

Lila Donnolo

I am hard pressed to describe how it could possibly be worse, in fact.

Owen

So, let's start with some, like, let's try to have a positive framing: What are some of the good parts of dying?

Lila Donnolo

Well, if you're in pain, then essentially, there's no more pain, but you know... nobody can corroborate that.

Owen

Have that problem again.

Lila Donnolo

Yes, yes, the reporting back

Owen

But essentially, if you had to guess the end of pain, at least like that? How would you rate that on a scale of 1 to 10?

Lila Donnolo

I mean, the end of pain is like excellent, you know, nine out of 10.

Owen

That's a nine out of 10, OK, and how about the other parts of the death experience?

Lila Donnolo

Oh, you mean like the gradually losing ability to use one’s organs…Voice?

Owen

That's, yes, that's exactly what I mean

Lila Donnolo

Ears, nose, mouth, thinking, cognition,

Owen

Oh gosh

Lila Donnolo

creativity, innovation

Owen

So all these things

Lila Donnolo

Pretty bad

Owen

So if you're reading the loss of your functioning on a scale from one to 10

Lila Donnolo

Oh yeah, that's a - 11

Owen

Oh, so you would not recommend it to someone else

Lila Donnolo

Would not recommend. I don't think most folks want to lose all of those wonderful capacities that we are given, having a body, as Rob Reni describes in paranoia, it's a pretty miraculous piece of machinery, a body. I'm not a real fan of the breaking down of my machinery or anyone else's.

Owen

Oh my God, so so real. I mean, ironically, like having a body would be a great customer experience if you even knew again when you're born, what you're being given.

Lila Donnolo

Oh my God, what a cool machine! You can run around you, you can jump, you can do so much! You can bounce off of things like parkour, you can have sex…

Owen

It does sound like there's a lot there, but to have that ripped away from you.

Lila Donnolo

You can masturbate! Oh my God, there's so much stuff you can do with the body.

Owen

Again, would you recommend the loss of these functions to a friend?

Lila Donnolo

Could not recommend

Owen

Ok

Lila Donnolo

bullshit— could not recommend

Owen

How about the speed of the experience? What do you feel like the customer service, like the promptness of response, was what you'd vote for?

Lila Donnolo

Yeah, so any speed of this experience generally is just heinous, whether it is sudden and unexpected, or whether it is drawn out over the course of years with slowly failing organs and a plethora of medications. All of the rates of speed are terrible.

Owen

I'm gonna put you down for it, “neither agree nor disagree”

Lila Donnolo

Where is terrible, go OK fine, whatever

Owen

It's either too fast or it's too slow, but both are bad

Lila Donnolo

Both are bad.

Owen

No rate of death is “good.”

Lila Donnolo

There is no Goldilocks death.

Owen

It's always a little, it's always somewhat wrong, or a lot wrong

Lila Donnolo

There is no just right unless you could do the illegal thing and choose the time of your death, in which case, perhaps the customer service experience would be slightly better.

Owen

It seems like they could focus more on the customer experience.

Lila Donnolo

Yeah, that would probably free up the agents’ time to focus on said customer service.

Owen

And by agent, you mean the reaper?… I hope this has been mildly therapeutic.

Lila Donnolo

This is delightful. I love you. Today, Viola, one of the hospice nurses who has been with me for four days in a row, I love her so much, she's like

“Did you ever look for that tray?”

I'm sitting on the couch, and I go… “No,” and she goes.

“You're not gonna look for it. I'm good. I'm gonna look for it cause if I don't do it, you're not.”

I was like— You're right. I'm not gonna do it.

Owen

Love you, bye-bye.

Lila Donnolo

I love you the most.

I include the audio of this conversation here, for posterity, and as “receipts or it didn’t happen points.”

I want to thank Lila for speaking with me during this difficult time.

You can read her work here:
